parts.move: state the path-difference conditions for constructive and destructive interference
parts.prompt: For two coherent in-phase sources, state the path-difference conditions for constructive and for destructive interference at a point.
scheme: Constructive: path difference = nλ (whole number of wavelengths), waves arrive in phase
Destructive: path difference = (n + ½)λ (odd number of half wavelengths), waves arrive in antiphase
n is any whole number: 0, 1, 2, …
parts.answer: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ, so the waves arrive in step; destructive interference occurs when it is an odd number of half wavelengths, (n+½)λ, so they arrive in antiphase and cancel.

parts.move: explain interference as the vector superposition of displacements
parts.prompt: Two waves of the same frequency meet at a point. Explain, in terms of displacement addition, what determines whether the point is bright, dark, or intermediate.
scheme: The resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements at each instant
In phase, crests meet crests: maximum amplitude — bright (or loud)
In antiphase, crests meet troughs: zero resultant — dark (or silent); between, partial cancellation gives intermediate intensity
parts.answer: Displacements add as vectors: at each instant the resultant is the sum of the two waves' displacements. In phase, crest meets crest and the amplitude — and intensity — is maximal; in antiphase, crest meets trough and they cancel to darkness; anything between superposes to an intermediate value.

parts.move: explain why a stable two-source pattern needs both coherence and overlap
parts.prompt: Explain why two headlight beams crossing on a road do not produce a visible interference pattern, while two coherent laser beams do.
scheme: Interference needs a fixed phase relationship at every point — coherence
Headlights have unrelated phases that drift randomly, so any fringe pattern flickers and averages away
Lasers maintain a fixed phase relation, so the same places stay bright or dark long enough to see
parts.answer: Interference happens physically in both cases, but a stable visible pattern requires the phase relationship at each point to stay fixed. Headlights drift through random relative phases, so their interference fringes flicker past invisibly fast and average out; coherent laser beams hold their phase relation, freezing the pattern in place.

parts.move: compute a path difference and classify the interference outcome
parts.prompt: Two coherent loudspeakers emit 0.68 m wavelength sound. A listener is 4.76 m from one speaker and 5.44 m from the other. Determine the path difference and state whether the listener hears a maximum or a minimum.
scheme: Path difference = 5.44 − 4.76 = 0.68 m
0.68 m = 1 × 0.68 m = 1λ, a whole number of wavelengths
Whole λ → waves arrive in phase → constructive, a loud spot
parts.answer: The path difference is 5.44 − 4.76 = 0.68 m, exactly one wavelength. The waves arrive in phase, so the listener sits at a constructive maximum — a loud spot.

parts.move: use the fringe geometry in reverse to find a distance to a minimum
parts.prompt: Microwaves of wavelength 3.0 cm pass through two slits 6.0 cm apart. A detector 2.0 m away moves sideways from the centre line. Calculate the distance from the centre to the first minimum.
scheme: First minimum needs path difference λ/2 = 1.5 cm
Path difference ≈ dx/L for small angles: x = (λ/2)L/d
parts.answer: The first minimum needs a half-wavelength path difference of 1.5 cm. With x = λL/2d, the detector finds it at x = (0.015×2.0)/0.060 = 0.50 m from the centre line — a large, easy-to-locate dead spot because the wavelength is centimetres, not nanometres.

parts.move: reject the idea that destructive interference destroys energy
parts.prompt: A student says dark fringes prove that energy has been destroyed where the waves cancel. Explain where the energy actually goes.
scheme: Interference only redistributes energy; total energy is conserved
The energy missing from dark fringes reappears as brighter bright fringes
Averaged over the whole pattern, the total energy equals the sum of what each source delivers alone
parts.answer: Nothing is destroyed: interference redistributes energy. The light missing from dark fringes is redirected into the bright ones — averaged over the whole pattern the energy delivered equals the sum of the two sources' contributions. Cancellation at one point is always paid for by reinforcement elsewhere.

parts.move: reject ignoring a source phase inversion when computing path difference
parts.prompt: One of two otherwise identical coherent sources vibrates in antiphase with the other (π out of phase). A student claims the centre of the pattern must be bright because the path difference there is zero. Explain the error.
scheme: Zero path difference leaves the sources' built-in π phase difference uncompensated
The waves arrive in antiphase at the centre — a dark fringe
The whole pattern inverts: old minima become maxima and vice versa
parts.answer: Path difference is only half the story: the sources themselves differ by π. At the centre, zero path difference preserves that inversion, so the waves arrive in antiphase and cancel — the centre is dark, and every fringe of the usual pattern swaps role.

parts.move: transfer interference counting to measuring a tiny displacement
parts.prompt: In a Michelson-type setup, moving one mirror by 0.12 μm shifts the pattern from one bright fringe to the next-but-one (two fringes). Calculate the wavelength of the light, explaining the factor of two.
scheme: A mirror displacement d changes the round-trip path by 2d
Two fringe shifts = two half-wavelength changes: 2d = 2×(λ/2)
λ = 2d/2 = d = 0.12 μm — wait: two fringes mean 2d = 2λ, so λ = d = 0.12 μm; check: 2d = 0.24 μm = 2λ gives λ = 0.12 μm (120 nm, ultraviolet)
parts.answer: Moving a mirror by d lengthens the round trip by 2d. Two full fringe shifts mean 2d = 2λ, so λ = d = 0.12 μm (120 nm — an ultraviolet line). The factor of two is the round trip: the mirror counts twice.

parts.move: solve the Young geometry for a stated fringe spacing
parts.prompt: Coherent light of wavelength 480 nm passes through two slits 0.24 mm apart, forming fringes on a screen 1.5 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing. A student measures 12 fringe gaps across 30 mm — check this against your value.
scheme: Student: 30 mm/12 gaps = 2.5 mm — close but ~17% off; re-measure or count again
Consistent within measurement error for an eyeball count
parts.answer: The predicted spacing is w = λD/d = 480×10⁻⁹×1.5/(0.24×10⁻³) = 3.0 mm. The student's 30/12 = 2.5 mm is 17% low — probably a miscounted fringe or an edge-of-fringe reading. The two values agree only marginally; the count should be repeated.

parts.move: combine path-difference geometry with photon energy at a bright fringe
parts.prompt: A 500 nm two-source interference pattern has a bright fringe where the total light intensity is 3.0×10⁻³ W m⁻². Calculate the photon arrival rate per square metre at that fringe. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: Rate = intensity/E = 3.0×10⁻³/3.98×10⁻¹⁹
≈ 7.5×10¹⁵ photons s⁻¹ m⁻²
parts.answer: Each 500 nm photon carries E = hc/λ = 3.98×10⁻¹⁹ J. The bright fringe intensity 3.0×10⁻³ W m⁻² therefore corresponds to 3.0×10⁻³/3.98×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 7.5×10¹⁵ photons arriving per second per square metre — the wave picture's intensity in the photon picture's counting rate.

parts.move: combine interference detection with a feedback application in a CD player
parts.prompt: A CD player's tracking system uses two reflected beams that interfere: when the lens is centred on the track, the detector sees a particular brightness; drifting off-track changes the path difference and the detected intensity. Explain how interference converts a tiny tracking error into a large electrical signal, and why the method is sensitive.
scheme: Off-track drift changes one beam's path relative to the other by a fraction of a wavelength
The phase difference moves the detector along the interference fringe curve
Near a steep part of a fringe, a sub-wavelength shift produces a large intensity change
The system senses errors far smaller than the light wavelength because fringe positions are wavelength-precise
parts.answer: As the lens drifts, the two reflected beams' path difference changes by a fraction of a wavelength, sliding the detector across the interference fringes. Because fringe edges are steep, a drift of a few per cent of λ swings the detected intensity strongly — the interferometer converts sub-wavelength geometry into a large, fast electrical signal, which the servo feeds back to re-centre the lens.
